items.title: Snapdragons disprove Mendel's simplest law in one cross
items.claim: Red snapdragon crossed with white snapdragon. Mendel's dominance rule says: offspring should all be red (or all white). Snapdragon offspring are PINK. The textbook law fails on its very first test.

options.text: Mendel's laws don't apply to plants

Incomplete dominance — heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype because neither allele fully masks the other; the red allele encodes a pigment enzyme, and one functional copy produces only half as much pigment as two
Pink is a separate allele not from either parent

items.reveal:
Mendel happened to choose seven traits in peas that were all controlled by single genes with full dominance and complete penetrance. Most real traits are not.

Incomplete dominance: heterozygotes show intermediate phenotypes. Pink snapdragons. Pink camellias. Light pink human skin (one functional MC1R copy).

Codominance: both alleles fully expressed simultaneously. Human ABO blood group (a person with A and B alleles has both A and B antigens on red cells).

Epistasis: gene A's effect depends on gene B's genotype. Coat colour in Labradors (E gene controls whether B gene's brown/black is visible at all).

Polygenic inheritance: traits like height controlled by hundreds of small-effect genes. Family resemblance plus 'regression to the mean'.

Real genetics is much richer than 'dominant masks recessive'.
items.why: Mendel's laws are presented as universal. They describe a subset of inheritance patterns. Even simple breeding shows the laws don't always apply directly.

items.title: Species are vanishing 100 to 1000 times faster than normal
items.claim: The fossil record gives a 'background' extinction rate: roughly 1 species per million per year. Current rates are 100 to 1000 times that — and rising. Many biologists call it the sixth mass extinction.

options.text: Asteroid impact like 66 million years ago
Habitat destruction (especially tropical deforestation), invasive species, climate change, pollution and overharvesting — a multi-cause anthropogenic mass extinction with no single dominant mechanism

items.reveal:
The five previous mass extinctions (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous) each saw 50-95% of species disappear over geological timescales. The Permian was the worst — ~96% of marine species lost over ~60,000 years.

The current rate, calculated from documented vertebrate extinctions (Ceballos, Ehrlich and others), is 100-1000 times background. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017, Krefeld study) show 75% reductions over 27 years in German nature reserves.

Human impacts: forest cover reduced by ~30% globally since 1700; ocean fish biomass down ~50% since 1970; freshwater vertebrates down 84% (WWF Living Planet Report). Climate change adds an accelerating layer.

Protected areas and conservation work — by some measures, extinction rates would have been 4x higher without them.

Mass extinctions reshape evolution for tens of millions of years. We won't return to the world we know within human-relevant timeframes — the species we lose are lost.
items.why: Species loss feels gradual. The rate is geological in magnitude — comparable to events that left fossil-record-defining boundaries. We are living through one.

items.title: A woman who died in 1951 still has dividing cells today
items.claim: Normal human cells divide about 50 times and then stop (the Hayflick limit). HeLa cells, taken from Henrietta Lacks's cervical tumour in 1951, divide indefinitely. They are in laboratories on every continent.

options.text: Constitutive expression of telomerase — the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres on chromosome ends — allows them to divide without losing telomeric DNA, bypassing the Hayflick limit. The HPV-derived oncogenes E6 and E7 also disable normal tumour suppressors
Special preservation chemicals keep them alive
All cancer cells are technically immortal

items.reveal_title: Telomeres, telomerase, and the loophole around cell senescence
items.reveal:
Linear chromosomes lose a small amount of DNA from their ends with each replication (the 'end replication problem'). Once telomeres reach a critical short length, cells trigger senescence — the Hayflick limit, named after Leonard Hayflick (1961).

Most adult cells suppress telomerase. Germline cells, stem cells and most cancers reactivate it. HeLa cells express telomerase robustly. Combined with disabled tumour suppressors (p53 and Rb, neutralised by HPV-18 oncoproteins), they grow without limit.

HeLa cells were the first immortal human cell line. They were taken without Henrietta Lacks's consent. The ethical legacy is still being addressed — her family didn't learn the cells existed until 1973, and only signed an agreement with the NIH on access to her genome in 2013.
items.why: Cell death is taught as inevitable. The cellular machinery to bypass it exists; cancer cells exploit it; HeLa cells made it visible.
